figures.caption: ◾ FIGURE 11.1 The flow of genetic information according to the central dogma of molecular biology. Replication, transcription, and translation occur in all organisms; reverse transcription occurs in cells infected with certain RNA viruses. The transfer of information from RNA to RNA during the replication of RNA viruses is not shown.
figures.depicts: Flow chart titled 'The Central Dogma'. A horizontal arrow labelled '1. Perpetuation of genetic information from generation to generation' runs from a DNA double helix (with a TTT/AAA base-pair inset) through 'Replication — DNA-dependent DNA polymerase' to two daughter DNA helices. A vertical arrow labelled '2. Control of the phenotype: Gene expression' runs down from DNA through 'Transcription — DNA-dependent RNA polymerase' (green arrow) to an mRNA carrying UUU, with a red reverse arrow labelled 'Reverse transcription — RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase)', then 'Translation — complex process involving ribosomes, tRNAs, and other molecules' (orange arrow) to a polypeptide ending in Phe.

figures.caption: ◾ FIGURE 11.10 Mechanism of rho-independent termination of transcription. As transcription proceeds along a DNA template, a region of DNA is encountered that contains inverted repeat sequences (shaded). When these repeat sequences are transcribed, the RNA transcript will contain sequences that are complementary to each other. As a result, they will hydrogen bond and form a hairpin structure. When RNA polymerase encounters this hairpin, it will pause, and the weak hydrogen bonds between the A's that follow in the template strand and the U's in the newly synthesized transcript will break, releasing the transcript from the DNA.
figures.depicts: A four-stage sequence-level diagram of rho-independent termination: a DNA duplex with shaded 'Inverted repeat sequences' and 'Six adenines' (yellow) on the template strand; Step 1 transcription of the inverted repeats; Step 2 transcription of six A's and rapid folding of the green RNA transcript into a hydrogen-bonded hairpin (the stem base pairs listed, loop U-C-C) with an 'Area of weak hydrogen bonding' (UUUUUU opposite AAAAAA); Step 3 release of the transcript when RNA polymerase pauses after hairpin formation, the freed RNA ending UUUUUU-OH-3′.

figures.caption: ◾ FIGURE 11.13 Structure of a promoter recognized by RNA polymerase II. The TATA and CAAT boxes are located at about the same positions in the promoters of most nuclear genes encoding proteins. The GC and octamer boxes may be present or absent; when present, they occur at many different locations, either singly or in multiple copies. The sequences shown here are the consensus sequences for each of the promoter elements. The conserved promoter elements are shown at their locations in the mouse thymidine kinase gene.

figures.caption: ◾ FIGURE 11.2 Gene expression involves two steps: transcription and translation, in both prokaryotes (a) and eukaryotes (b). In eukaryotes, the primary transcripts or pre-mRNAs often must be processed by the excision of introns and the addition of 5′ 7-methyl guanosine caps (Cap) and 3′ poly(A) tails [(A)n]. In addition, eukaryotic mRNAs must be transported from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where they are translated.

(b) Eukaryotic gene expression: inside a purple NUCLEUS a DNA line with Exon 1, Intron 1, Exon 2, Intron 2, Exon 3; Step 1 Transcription gives a primary transcript with Cap, AUG, UAA and A(n) tail; Step 2 Removal of introns (two loops fall out) gives mRNA; Step 3 Transport to cytoplasm; Step 4 Translation to a polypeptide in the CYTOPLASM.

figures.caption: ◾ FIGURE 11.9 Elongation of an RNA chain catalyzed by RNA polymerase in E. coli. (a) RNA polymerase is bound to DNA and is covalently extending the RNA chain. (b) RNA polymerase has moved downstream from its position in (a), processively extending the nascent RNA chain.
figures.depicts: Two panels of RNA polymerase (tan blob) on a DNA double helix: (a) the enzyme bound to DNA covalently extending the green growing RNA chain, with labels 'Site for incoming ribonucleoside triphosphate', 'Rewinding site', 'Short region of DNA–RNA helix', 'Unwinding site'; (b) the enzyme moved downstream (dashed arrow 'Movement of RNA polymerase') with a longer growing RNA chain.

figures.caption: Isaacs Chapter 11b, slide 24 'Splicing: type 1' figure (Principles of Genetics 4/e Fig 11-25): a tRNA precursor with its intron sequence is cut at both ends by a splicing endonuclease (I), releasing the intron, and the two tRNA halves are joined by a splicing ligase (II) to give the mature tRNA.
figures.depicts: A four-stage line drawing of a cloverleaf tRNA: 'tRNA precursor' (purple, 5′ P and 3′ OH ends) with a red-shaded 'Intron sequence' in the anticodon arm; arrow 'I Splicing endonuclease' → the intron (red, HO 5′ … P 3′) falls out leaving two tRNA halves with free OH and P ends; arrow 'II Splicing ligase' → the halves are joined into the 'Mature tRNA'. Credit: Figure 11-25 Principles of Genetics, 4/e © 2006 John Wiley & Sons.

figures.caption: TABLE 11.1 Characteristics of the Five RNA Polymerases of Eukaryotes. Enzyme / Location / Products: RNA polymerase I — Nucleolus — Ribosomal RNAs, excluding 5S rRNA. RNA polymerase II — Nucleus — Nuclear pre-mRNAs. RNA polymerase III — Nucleus — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and other small nuclear RNAs. RNA polymerase IV — Nucleus (plant) — Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). RNA polymerase V — Nucleus (plant) — Some siRNAs plus noncoding (antisense) transcripts of siRNA target genes.
